utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There is something I would like to clarify before we start this morning. In reviewing the transcript for last week over the weekend, I was reminded of a hurried intervention when accused and counsel appeared to be speaking loudly at the same time when I made reference to puppetry. I -- it concerned me when I re-read it that it could be regarded as a general comment and not confined to that particular occasion, so forth avoidance of any doubt whatsoever, I want to say one thing. I hope, indeed I think, that counsel know that I appreciate the responsible way in which the proceedings have been handled in general by counsel and that the comment was one made in the heat of the moment. Can we now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind during that and the rest of the day that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mijatovic [sic]. You told us that after David Gajic left that your new boss, the coordinator was Mr. Vilotic. How many of you were working directly under Mr. Vilotic? I understood you were his deputy but were you his only deputy or were you one of several?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another deputy there who was involved in counter-intelligence in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was that? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these people changed during these eight years. Several of them came for one-year or six-month stints. The last one who was there when the war broke out was Slobodan Milikic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Since you were the one who was there the longest, were you considered the number-two man?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us on Friday in your direct examination that when a crime was uncovered by the service, especially crimes relating to terrorism, the state service would investigate and do preliminary investigations, would interview people. Did you yourself personally interview any of those persons arrested?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally. Perhaps at the very outset. As for some of the work we did in 1993 and 1994, on one or three occasions I personally took part, but usually it was the operatives from the centre of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And at page 21942, one of your answers was that no one from the public security sector was in charge of anything or could issue any orders in the state security sector. I have a question. Given the level you were at, how -- how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that first of all in terms of the rules of service. That is not allowed. And from my personal experience, I know that no one ever gave me any orders from any public security organ, and the rules of service say that that is not allowed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Couldn't the minister of interior delegate someone from public security to give information or give directions to DB personnel? Wasn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the practice that prevailed. Also, there was this instruction on the exchange of information that was adopted by the minister. So there was no need to convey that to anyone. According to the rules of service, one knew how one was supposed to work, and we knew who was entitled to issue orders to us, and that was only the head of the state security section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a topic I want to cover later, but I'll ask you a question about it right now. When you got involved in dealing with Mr. Rugova's situation during the war around the 31st of March, the 1st of April and following that, who gave you instructions or directions to go over and see Mr. Rugova and later on to transport him to and from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received information that Rugova was alive and that he was in his house, I consulted the immediate coordinator, Miso Vilotic, and we agreed I should go to his house and do what I did. After that, all the orders and everything that was supposed to be done was something that I was told by the chief of state security from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time that was Rade Markovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know from whom he was getting instructions, if any, regarding Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot know, but I can assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about David Gajic. When did he -- when did he leave his post as coordinator in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did Vilotic take up the position immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mijatovic [sic], do you know -- do you know why you were not promoted to that position? You had been the number-two guy in Kosovo for six or seven years; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Mr. Joksic that's on the stand, not Mr. Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I misspoke and I apologise, sir. Mr. Joksic, you know why you were not promoted to that position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say. Personnel policies were conducted by the chief of service, and it was his assessment that it should be Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And who was the chief of service who made that decision? Was it Stanisic or Markovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then specifically it was Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you leave Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 12th of June or July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether it's June or July. We with barely hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters just told us they couldn't -- couldn't hear you. Did you say June or July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: June. June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall when Jovica Stanisic was replaced by Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was during 1998, but I'm not quite sure. I think it was sometime in the month of October, October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what information did you have about why that took place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any information. We didn't have any information. I mean, who asked us down there who's going to be your boss? It was just changed and instead of Stanisic, Markovic came there. Why that happened, we really don't know. And no one told us why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- did David Gajic tell you why he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me. At that time people were saying that he was nearing the end of his career, that he was supposed to retire, and also it was being said that he should be involved in more peaceful work somewhere in the top echelons of the service, an easier job, because he was getting on in years. It was his age that was the main concern. He was rather sickly, too, and people were saying that that is why he was withdrawn to Belgrade, to get an easier job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Didn't David Gajic ever complain to you about this so-called Joint Command that was working in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he never told you that he thought that that body had been created because Milosevic was unhappy with the kind of information he was receiving from the -- from the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, didn't he actually get removed from his position as coordinator on or about the 1st of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He was down there until the end of December, and he was coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 21946 on Friday, you gave an answer that according to your information, neither David Gajic nor Mr. Vilotic were members of the MUP staff for Kosovo. That's your information, right, your understanding?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to the MUP staff in Kosovo, I'd like to show you a series of documents, and first can we start with P1251. This will be on the screen in a minute, Mr. Joksic. Actually, with the usher's help, let me hand you a hard copy. And if you'll look at the second page, you can see that this is -- this is from General Djordjevic, who I understand is on the public security side of the house. You see that signature and stamp on the second page?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this purportedly is on the 15th of May, 1998, and on the first page you'll see it's a decision on the formation of a Staff of the ministry in Pristina. Did you ever see that document before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If we could look next at P1252. And I'll give you a copy of that one as well. I'll trade you, if I may. The -- you'll see on the second page again this is another one from General Djordjevic, and the date may be difficult to read, but I think from other evidence it is the 11th of June, 1998. And you'll see on the front page this is a decision on the composition of the Staff. Did you see that document before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But most importantly, I want to show you P1505, and I'll hand you a copy of this one. This is dated the 16th of June, 1998. And this one is from the minister of the interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, and it's a decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism. Have you not seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you look on the first page you'll see it has General Sreten Lukic as the -- it's translated here as the head of staff, and David Gajic is listed as the deputy head of staff.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of this document signed by the minister?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to doubt the document as it -- I mean, that would be a matter of expertise. As far as I know, and I was down there all the time, David Gajic was never that. I know that Sreten Lukic's deputy was Miroslav Mijatovic. So David Gajic, as far as I know, well, I was down there but he was never the deputy of the head of this staff. I know that at that time Mijatovic was with Sreten Lukic as deputy head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how can you say that no members of the DB were on the MUP staff for Kosovo? This document's signed by the minister puts Mr. Gajic, who we all know was in the DB, as the deputy head.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's already twice given the factual bases for his answer, so I think that the counsel's question at this point is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask him another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Milorad Lukovic? You'll see him a couple names down, assistant head for special operations. He was DB. What's the source of your information that he's not on the staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know that Milorad Lukovic was a member of the staff. Later on during the war he showed up a few times down there. Probably -- well, I don't know. To the best of my knowledge he was not a member of the staff. Now, whether he was, I wasn't informed about it. I see that that is written here and it's written for Gajic, too, and I know for sure that he did not do that. Now, I mean what is written is another matter. As for Lukovic, then at that time I didn't even see him down there in Pristina at the time of this. I mean, in 19 -- well, during the war in 1999, I showed him -- I saw him show up a few times in Pristina, but I was not aware of this document. I never knew of the existence of this kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us -- I see Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me in respect to the transcript. Page 9, line 2. The witness said that in 1998 he did not see Lukovic at all, and then he saw him several times in 1999. That is what the witness said in actual effect, and perhaps it would be a good thing if my colleague Mr. Hannis would clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. We have great difficulty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you want to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Joksic, to the best of your memory Legija, or Milorad Lukovic was only in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1998 I did not see him in Kosovo. In 1999, during the NATO bombing and during the war then I saw him two or three times. He did show up in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how can you be certain you did not see him in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999 I did. I did not see him in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question is how can you be sure that you did not see him in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't see him. Well, I mean, I was down there all the time. And Pristina is not a big city so that you would not see or notice if he'd come. And I was there at the SUP and at the service. So I did not see him in 1998. And in 1999, I saw him about two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as you said, Pristina is -- is fairly small. In 1998 did you not see Mr. Sainovic in Pristina on numerous occasions in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Sainovic several times, but most of all on television rather than in direct contacts in 1998. As far as I know, at that time, to the best of my knowledge, he was in charge of contacts with foreign missions, diplomats and others who were staying in Kosovo and Metohija. So it is in that capacity that I would see him every now and then. I did not have any personal contacts with him in 1998. It was only in 1999 that I did. But I saw him in Pristina because it's a small town, and the TV was still working then and newspapers were writing about him meeting with various foreign officials in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not also see Mr. Minic and Mr. Matkovic in Pristina in 1998, because they, along with Mr. Sainovic, attended dozens of meetings in Pristina between July and October 1998.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And those other two politicians, I saw them, too, coming every now and then to Pristina. As for their specific assignments as politicians, well, I wasn't informed exactly why they were coming and in what capacity. I knew that Minic was president of, I think, one of the chambers of the Federal Assembly. So it was probably in that capacity. Matkovic, as far as I know, was the director of Sartid and an official of the SPS, but I saw them coming there two or three times. I saw them meeting up with the local politicians there in Kosovo and Metohija and with the mayor and with the president of the provisional executive council of Kosovo and Metohija and these other people, but I noticed that sort of in passing two or three times. I saw them there in Pristina two or three times, but they stayed for a very short while and they'd leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And neither Mr. David Gajic or Mr. Radovic from your service told you about meeting with those politicians and representatives of the public security and the VJ in Pristina in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for these meetings that David Gajic attended and Miroslav Radovic, too, well, I knew about them because we in the service would prepare information that they were exchanging there, and I knew that they had meetings with members of the army and the public security. It is for that purpose that we prepared for them all this information that we were receiving from the ground so that they could present this information at these meetings. Directly who took part in these meetings, well, Gajic did not convey that to me. He didn't talk about it, and there was no need to. We knew what our job was. So we were supposed to exchange the information that we had available so that all the rest who were in charge of security in -- of security in Kosovo and Metohija could go on acting in a coordinated manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, what you're saying is you don't know if these meetings Gajic went to were attended by these political people, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, and Mr. Matkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, still looking at this Exhibit P1505 from the 16th of June, you'll see here under Lukovic two names down we have the assistant head for special police units. I take it that's the PJP; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says assistant head of staff special police units, Major Goran Radosavljevic. I could not really interpret this, what it means special police units. I know that the PJP was there. Now, whether that pertains to the PJP, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we had two names above Milorad Lukovic for special operations, and you know that was the JSO; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And right. Below that, we have Lieutenant Colonel Trajkovic, assistant head for special anti-terrorist units. That's the SAJ, isn't it, S-A-J?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next logical thing in describing the units of the police would be the PJP, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the PJP, but I really could not be the Judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us on Friday that as far as you knew Goran Radosavljevic didn't -- didn't command any units. I think you told us as far as you knew he was only in charge of training; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1999. I didn't know about this in 1998, but in 1999, as far as I was told then, as far as I knew then, he was a member of the staff or assistant head of staff for the training of special police units. That's what I had been told, and that's how I knew of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember now exactly who it was that told me. A member of the staff, someone from the staff. But the members of the staff, those who are written here, I mean apart from him I didn't see any of these others who are listed in this decision. Zivko Trajkovic, he did not come. He came rarely. Lukovic in 1999, as I already mentioned two or three times. Only Goran Radosavljevic was there more often as a member of the staff. It was completely different people. Mijatovic and five or six other people were on the staff. In this decision the names of those persons are not listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Joksic, do you allow for the possibility that these named members in the staff had meetings that you did not attend?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything about that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I see neither your name or Mr. Vilotic's name on this list.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's because we were never members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I tell you on the last page, item number 6 talks about with this decision coming into force, "the following shall come out of force," and rather than hand you the documents again, I will tell you that P1251 and P1252 that we looked at, I believe, are the ones referred to as the 15 May 1998 decision and the 11 June 1998 decision that were signed by Djordjevic. So it seems that the minister is -- is overriding what General Djordjevic on the public security side of the house had proposed and is creating this staff which includes both members of the DB as well as the JB. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document tells me that it's like that. However, I don't think had this ever got off the ground. It never began operating. This document you're showing me seems to suggest just that, but I can't say that I was ever aware of that. I didn't actually notice any of this in my work, not at any point, especially not the fact as is suggested here that David Gajic was the deputy chief of staff, as far as I knew. And I think I did know quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. One last thing before we leave this document. I think it's on the -- yeah, it's on page 2 of your B/C/S. Two paragraphs above item number 2. It says: "The expanded staff shall also include chiefs of the secretariats for internal affairs centres -- centres and branches of the RDB." You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you one last document related to this issue. It's P1811. I'll hand you a copy of that in just a second. Colonel, this is another document from the minister of the interior, and this one is dated the 31st of May, 1999. It's called a decision on establishment of the ministry staff. Did you ever see this document before today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise the people named there under General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, misrepresentation. Mr. Lukic never appointed these persons as members of the staff and we'll show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question is simply based on Lukic being at the top of the list and the others are under him. It's not suggesting, I don't think, command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the translation did. I was listening to the translation at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, it wasn't -- I gather from Mr. Hannis it wasn't meant to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was just asking if you recognise the names listed under General Lukic's name on this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise most of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were those people that worked with you and worked with the MUP in Pristina in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part except here it says "Deputy chief of the staff." Okay. This is the 31st of May, 1999. Yes, that's when Bozovic came to replace Mijatovic, and I do know all the other people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you go to the last page where we have the signature of -- of the minister of interior, item number 6 says this decision shall enter into force on the 1st of June, 1999, and then it says this decision supersedes the decision number 1580/98 of 16 June 1998 which I will tell you is the one that we were just looking at, Exhibit P1505. Now, reading that I take it to mean that the previous decision from 16 June 1998 had been in force until it was superseded by this one on the 31st of May, 1999. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question as phrased asks the witness to comment on what Mr. Hannis thinks. Whether what Mr. Hannis thinks is correct, I think that's improper. It's legal conclusion and best left for the trier of fact which in this case is the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that's something within the knowledge of this witness as a member of the Ministry of Interior whether a decision by the minister remains in effect unless and until it's replaced by a superseding decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think your question calls for him to draw the conclusion that Mr. Ivetic suggests. It may be a different question could be directed to whether on the face of it this is consistent with what happened in the -- in Kosovo during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I have a difficulty with that, given his previous answer regarding 1505 where he says as far as he knows, none of those guys were members of the staff. So it's hard to ask him if that's consistent with what he saw when the preceding document wasn't consistent with what he says he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but what would have been possible would be to say that the document you're now referring to, P1811, suggests that between -- is it May 1998 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 16 June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- June 1998 and the 1st of June 1999 the document 1505 and the personnel referred to in there were present, the document was in effect and these personnel were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that he sees that, does it not remind him what in fact was the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's factual matters alone that really this witness can deal with, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Joksic, that you had not seen this exhibit, P1811 or the previous one P1505 before coming here. Did you see any other decision from the minister of interior in -- between June 16th, 1998, and 31 May 1999 regarding the composition of the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And regarding the previous one that we looked at, was Colonel Trajkovic ever present in Pristina in 19 -- in the second half of 1998 and the first half of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Trajkovic, and I believe I do know about this, was a commander of the SAJ unit, which was a public security sector unit. I didn't know at the time whether he was a member of the staff, but we knew that he was the commander of this unit that was at the time in Kosovo Polje. I just saw that document which suggests that he was also a member of the staff, which I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see him physically present in Kosovo in the second half of 1998 and the first half of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see him over there, but I can't give you the day or the month that I did. I know that I used to see him in Kosovo now and again. They would travel back and forth between Kosovo and Belgrade. I do know for sure that during 1999, during the airstrikes, he did spend some time in Kosovo. As for these months that we're talking about now, I know that I saw him a couple of times. I can't tell you, though, whether it was the end of the year, the beginning of the year. It has been a long time, after all, and I can't say for sure. I know that I knew who Zivko Trajkovic was and I knew that he was the commander of the SAJ and I know that he did spend some time in Kosovo, he travelled to Kosovo, I know that much. And I also know that in 1999 during the air strikes he did spend time in Kosovo. As for earlier on, I did see him a couple of times but he came and went and I can't say exactly when I saw him because unit was not under my control and I didn't much keep track of what was going on over there. I do know that I did see him every now and again, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Major Radosavljevic? Was his nickname Gurij?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Gurij.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you not see Gurij in Kosovo in the second half of 1998 and the first half of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there during the airstrikes. I can't say about the preceding period of time. In the first half of 1999 I think he was actually in Kosovo, January and February, and March, and then the air-strikes started. Gurij was there. I did see him there. As for 1998, I can't really quite remember whether he was there all the time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another exhibit. This is P --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P2805. I'll hand you a copy of this one as well. This is described as the minutes of a meeting held on the 5th of November, 1998 at the ministry staff in Pristina. Have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This meeting was attended by the president of the republic of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, also by the minister of the interior, General Djordjevic, Rade Markovic, your boss Mr. Vilotic, David Gajic. You don't recall this meeting having taken place in early November 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that the President of Serbia came, but I can't remember the specific meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This looks like a pretty big meeting, a lot of people attending, a lot of important people attending, including General Pavkovic and 13 representatives of the Pristina Corps. Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, Mr. Matkovic. Wasn't this a big event at the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hardly my place to say whether it was big or small. I know that the president came to tour Kosovo after everything that had gone on in 1998. It was probably a big one. I'm looking at the list and there was quite many of them, but I can't say anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see among the people attending is Goran Radosavljevic. Do you see his name? I think it's the second name after Colonel Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory about whether he was in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I for one can't remember. This suggests that he was there. He probably was there. Was he there throughout, I really can't say. I know about 1999, that he was. As for 1998, I did see him every now and then, but I can't specifically remember. He probably was because that's what the document claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Petrovic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I see that it has been corrected. I believed there was a problem but there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, near -- near the end of the list of people attending, it mentions the chiefs of the CRDB. Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chiefs of the state security centre in Kosovo were in Pristina, Milan Lakovic in Prizren, Milivoje Savic, Bozidar Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what is ORDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are departments of the service, and these are parts of the centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how many people would that be in November of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a department in Kosovska Mitrovica, one in Urosevac, one in Pec and one in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a total of four. Kresin Jakovic had belonged to Prizren, Urosevac belonged to Gnjilane, and Kosovska Mitrovica belonged to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the fourth department you listed Jakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you personally did not attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I wasn't. My name is not there but can't remember. I see that all the heads of the centres were there and departments, so I was supposed to be there. I should have been there. Why wasn't I? Maybe I was away on that day. I know the meeting took place. I see that was I there, no, I wasn't; why wasn't I there, I don't know why I wasn't. I should have been there. Maybe I simply forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you keep any kind of official diary during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where that diary is today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was destroyed when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How about -- did you keep personal diary, a non-official diary?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you don't have any contemporaneous notes or accounts of where you were or what was happening with you in 1998 and 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer have any. I did have something like that when I was still an active employee of the state security sector. According to our rules of service, this sort of thing is handed over when you retire and probably destroyed. I don't think I would have been allowed anyway to -- to continue to keep these as private documents in my possession. I think I probably would have been prosecuted for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In the list of people attending where it has David Gajic and Milisav Miletic [sic], my English translation says RDB assistant chiefs. As I understood, you told us Vilotic didn't start until 1 January and Gajic left at the end of December 1998. Do you know why both of them were attending this meeting in November?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milisav Vilotic, was the assistant chief of sector in Belgrade. There had been decision to that effect. He came to Kosovo in late December 1997 [Realtime transcript read in error "Steven"]. He was supposed to replace Gajic back then. However, Gajic stayed on for another year, and Vilotic remained in Kosovo as assistant chief or head of the sector. He stuck around. He helped with the work of the centres. He did not hold any official post for that year apart from being the assistant head, but he remained in Kosovo for another year with no specific official post. He had arrived in Kosovo in late December 1997. What it says here assistants and so on, Gajic and Vilotic, pursuant to this decision they were both assistant heads of the sector at the service's HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the transcript has some references to Miletic which should be Vilotic. For example, in line 7 of page 22, line 12. There's no doubt you're referring to Vilotic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know if I misspoke, but that's what I intended, and I think we all understand that's who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in Line 14 at the beginning the transcript shows late December Stevan I believe it was 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while Mr. Hannis is mentioning the English translation of the document I note the English translation of the document does have a significant error. In the paragraph where it says -- in the introductory paragraph where it says Major-General Sreten Lukic, in the Serbian version it says Major-General Sreten Lukic and Major-General Momcilo Stojanovic, who of course is from the VJ, and then it lists Mijatic [phoen], Vucurevic, Radosavljevic, Zdravkovic, Adamovic, Slovic, Rajcic, Krstic and Vuckovic, staff members, and then it goes on to list other persons present who were not staff members. It's a critical translation issue so if -- I don't know if we need to have the CLSS verify what -- what I say there's a missing -- there's a missing word in there that does change the meaning somewhat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that there's a word used in the B/C/S version that's omitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Between Major-General Sreten Lukic and Major-General Momcilo Stojanovic there is what would be the English translation of "and."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we can have that rectified as you suggest, but how does it alter the meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Serbian when you say Major-General Sreten Lukic and Momcilo Stojanovic, then there's a pause and then you list persons and say staff members, it separates the Major-General Lukic and Major-General Momcilo Stojanovic from persons who are listed as staff members so it makes a -- it's a minor difference but I did want to bring it to the attention since it is a document that counsel seems to be interested in and is relying upon the English translation of, but clearly Gajic and Vilotic are down as other participants and not as staff members, which I think is of some import.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis you should resubmit this document to CLSS. It obviously can be done very quickly since it's one word we're talking about. Well, perhaps it's not as simple as that. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 23, line 12, my learned friend Mr. Hannis talked about Stojanovic who is, of course, from the VJ. Why the "of course," since we don't know who this is a reference to and it's certainly not the Stojanovic from the VJ since at the time he was no major general. Back in 1998 he was a mere colonel. And if you look at the evidence, that's what it clearly shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your quarrel is with Mr. Ivetic and not with Mr. Hannis on that score. It's Mr. Ivetic who is making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The transcript records otherwise, Your Honours. That's just what I was going to step up for. It is my words, and I did misspeak about it being that Stojanovic. There's another Stojanovic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But is it a VJ Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we agreed on that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you can make the appropriate filing once that's back to CLSS, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, I would ask you to look at one other thing in this document. On the first page in your hard copy about seven lines up from the bottom of that page you'll see a reference to the 27th of October, 1998. I want to ask you about the sentence that follows that, and this is President Milutinovic speaking. He says that on the 29th of October, 1998, a meeting with the -- with the FRY president was held regarding the situation within the army and the police. Did you -- were you aware of a body called the operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija? Do you have any knowledge of that body?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And with reference to that meeting, which I would suggest to Your Honours is the meeting described in Exhibit P2166, if you could go to the second page in B/C/S and it's the fifth line down. Mr. -- perhaps the fourth line down. Mr. Milutinovic says: "Everything remains the same for the Yugoslav army and police, Joint Command. VJ units are not withdrawing and police forces are reduced only by the part that has already been withdrawn." It seems that President Milutinovic is aware of the Joint Command but you and the RDB in Kosovo were not aware of it? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not aware that General Lukic attended a meeting of the interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo on the 29th of October in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I know that he went up there for some reason, but I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know of a person named Milorad Jankovic in -- in the MUP in 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Jankovic? No, I can't remember. I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another document. This is Exhibit P1693, and this is -- this is from the 1st of May, 1999. I'll hand you a hard copy. This appears to be a survey or report of events in -- regarding the security situation between the 30th of April and the 1st of May, 1999. You see the last page has General Lukic's name. Is this a routine document that was submitted to the minister of the interior and the chiefs of the RDB and the RJB in 1999 during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- it's a routine overview of events for that day in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall having seen this particular document before today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you generally receive these documents in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember receiving them or seeing that document accidentally at the staff. I see that information is contained here that was provided by the service concerning the SUPs and the officers in charge so that our data is included here as well, but we went through this document where the staff reported what had happened the previous day in Kosovo and Metohija. I didn't receive this document individually. It wasn't copied to me. You can see who the addressees are. But occasionally it's possible that I saw it at the staff. I didn't see it being drafted, certainly, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the persons it's addressed to is Colonel Krstic as head of the analytical administration. Was he in Belgrade at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And based on what you've said just before, I gather that you or your -- your group had input -- I mean, some of the information contained here is information that would have come from -- from you and your guys; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The procedure was as follows: Chiefs of centres in Kosovo and Metohija would get certain intelligence, and they would pass it on to us for purposes of coordination. We would assess it. If something was purely local, we would tell them, "Inform the chief of SUP what's going on in his territory," or he would do that of his own accord. Sometimes when some information reached us that was more important we as being in charge of state security coordination, we would inform the staff of what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija if some major terrorist attacks were expected, but for the most part, chiefs of centres would inform chiefs of SUPs, and whenever they informed us they would make a point of saying we had informed the chief of SUP or the garrison on that territory in case the army needs to be informed or involved that they should be in the know. That's how it was during peacetime. When the war began in Kosovo all that stopped and reporting was very difficult. We did as best as we could manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look at the last page, item number 4. It refers to persons who fled the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Do you see that? And the third paragraph, the last one before -- before item number 5 says between 24 April and 30 April 1999 a total of 715.158 persons belonging to the Siptar national minority left the territory of the FRY. 517.000 via Vrbnica, et cetera. Were you aware of that information in April of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was aware of this specific information. I can't remember. But we knew that people of all ethnicities were leaving the territory at the beginning of the war, and we knew that members of the Albanian minority community started leaving Kosovo and Metohija en masse after the start of the air-strikes. They went primarily to Albania and Macedonia. I was aware of this specific information that day. I just can't recall precisely the day. I know that a large number of ethnic Albanians left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at the beginning of the war just as Serbs did and people of other ethnicities. They even started leaving before the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about an answer you gave on Friday at page 21950. Mr. -- I think it was Mr. Ivetic was talking to you about the JSO. You said that you had no direct -- no connection with that unit and you thought they were stationed about four or five kilometres away from Kosovska Mitrovica. You said that unit was directly linked to the chief of service and they had almost no connection with us. The chief of service in 1999 would have been Rade Markovic; right? That's who you mean the JSO had a direct connection with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any information or hear anything about the JSO being deployed to Dubrava prison in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object insofar as Dubrava prison is a specific site that has been dropped from our indictment. If the counsel is wishing to bring that up, I submit that we'll have a lot more work before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just asking if they were deployed there. It has to do with command and control and who is dealing with. I'm not asking about what happened there, not at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That appears to be consistent with what has happened in relation to at least one other site. So with that undertaking, Mr. Hannis, you may proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, do you recall the question or should I ask it again?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any information or hear anything about the JSO being deployed to Dubrava prison in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such information. I had the information that I mentioned on Friday, that they were deployed four to five kilometres of Kosovska Mitrovica, but to date I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer you said, "They had almost no connection with us." So that sounds like they had some connection with you, however slight. What was that connection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had no connection with us whatsoever. It was the chief of sector who was directly in charge of commanding over them, and we had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could the minister of interior not issue an order to the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about during a state of war? Could not the Supreme Command or Mr. Milosevic issue an order to the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't think they could. I know that according to our rules the unit was responsible only to the chief of sector. Except the chief of sector, I don't believe anyone was able to directly command the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that in a previous period before 1998 and 1999, this is at page 21951 in the transcript: "We as members of the service could ask the chief of the RDB, if we were carrying out a complex action, to have a part of the JSO engaged in it. I think this occurred on only two or three occasions throughout my stay from 1992 to 1999." What -- what changed prior to 1998 and 1999? Couldn't you in 1998 and 1999 still request the chief of the RDB to have the JSO engaged?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we know the chief of -- the service of state security gathers operative intelligence. They don't conduct armed operations against terrorists. And in years before 1998 and 1999, for instance if we had intelligence that there was an armed group that ordinary police units could not tackle and arrest, that it's likely they would put up a lot of resistance and kill a lot of people, then 10 or 15 men from a specialised unit would come to arrest the suspected terrorists and that's how the job would be done. That's what we could do then. In 1998 and 1999, we couldn't do it the same way because the situation was different. There was an armed insurgency by terrorists, and all other units were engaged to combat them, not our service. Why would our service do it? Half [Realtime transcript read in error "happen"] of our personnel don't even know how to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the guys in JSO know how to shoot; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the best trained unit for combatting terrorism out of all those we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the JSO was engaged in anti-terrorist operations in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo, in joint operations with the VJ; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, but probably. I don't know specifically where they were engaged and how, because we had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a transcript issue, Your Honours. Page 31, line 9, "happen," I believe should be "half of" instead of "happen of."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you -- you weren't aware of the JSO being engaged in any of those anti-terrorist operations in Kosovo. I take it then you don't know who would have coordinated their being engaged in joint operations with the VJ, do you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but according to the rules it should be the chief of sector. I don't know, however, who coordinated in specific operations. It was probably the chief. It couldn't have been anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You said on -- on Friday that other than perhaps one JSO reserve officer being involved in -- in an individual killing that you were not aware of any other crimes committed by members of the JSO in Kosovo in the course of 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to the 17th of May, 1999, did you receive any request from -- from the deputy minister Rade Markovic or anyone from his office for information about crimes that the JSO might have been involved in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we received that request. In fact, we surely didn't. They couldn't request it from us because we didn't know anything about that as members of the service in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how about the presence of Arkan's in Kosovo in 1999? Is that something your service would have been aware of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not aware of the presence of Arkan's men in Kosovo and Metohija until I saw some statements in this trial saying that they were there. All I can say is that there were no Arkan's men in Pristina. The only thing that's possible, although I don't know this, that they were in the reserve forces of the JSO but that the state security sector knew they were in Kosovo and Metohija. Outside reserve JSO units, we didn't know. I know that there was some sort of staff in the Grand Hotel, since I lived there in some hidden basis during the air-strikes I know that there was no staff of Arkan's men in the Grand Hotel. But in 1992, seven years before the war when Arkan was doing his electoral campaign in Kosovo, their entire staff was in the Grand Hotel, and at that time five deputies were elected from Kosovo and Metohija, but that was an electoral campaign headquarters in the Grand Hotel in 1992, not during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 32, line 25. It says: "I know there was some staff in the Grand Hotel." There's a whole passage missing. The witness actually said that during proofing he found out that some people were saying that during the war there was some sort of staff or headquarters in the Grand Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you wish to clarify that? The answer seems to be translated in a way that doesn't reflect the whole of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, you've heard the discussion that just took place. Can you clarify for us what your answer was about a staff in the Grand Hotel during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war there was no headquarters of Arkan's men in the Grand Hotel, and I said, although you didn't ask me that, that he had an electoral headquarters in 1992 when he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got that. We got that answer. The question was whether there was any other staff office in the Grand Hotel. Forget about Arkan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We who were legal occasionally used the basement of the Grand Hotel to hold meetings after the air-strikes when the MUP building in Pristina was destroyed. That's down there underground in the basement of the Grand Hotel. That's where we met a few times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've been translated as saying we who were legal occasionally used the basement of the Grand Hotel to hold meetings after the air strikes in Pristina. What did you actually say? It doesn't sound right in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the army, the MUP staff, and I as a member of the service of state security met there, held meetings there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the witness in his first answer did say "we who were legal."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of meetings did you have in the basement with the army in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not official meetings. It was in the evenings, because all of us had our bases where we hid during the war. We would meet up there but only after the MUP was hit during air-strikes. We would meet there to exchange information about what had happened that day in Kosovo and Metohija. It was not an official sort of meeting. We just exchanged information about where air-strikes had been during that day, what had happened, and sometimes we had dinner there, all of us. So those were not official meetings with minutes kept. We just told each other the latest news, and we made a point of splitting up as early as possible so as --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so as not to get killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 34, lines 24, we would meet there to exchange information. He said the number of times and it wasn't -- I don't want to suggest the answer. Maybe we could ask him how many times and it will be clear without me suggesting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many times you're talking about, Mr. Joksic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't recall exactly how many times. Two or three times, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any civilians attend any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who from the -- who from the VJ attended these meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were two or three times when Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic attended. Sometimes this security officer would come with them, Momir Stojanovic. I'm not sure. I think Momir was there because we directly exchanged information, the two of us. And on behalf of the staff, the chief, Lukic, represented the staff. I was there as member of the state security and Miso Miletic -- Vilotic. Correction. Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it just the three of you then from the MUP, Lukic and Vilotic and yourself? Anybody else from MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so at these briefings. They were short, 10, 15 minutes for purposes of exchanging information. I don't know. Perhaps occasionally somebody would come from the staff if they needed to bring some sort of information, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not aware of a 17 May 1999 meeting that Rade Markovic attended with President Milosevic, Mr. Sainovic, General Ojdanic and other representatives from the army to discuss certain alleged crimes by members of both the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said you became aware after, through some statements made at this trial about some of that. Were you aware there's evidence in this case that Rade Markovic reported at that meeting that Arkan had offered a hundred volunteers but that he had only taken 30 of them, and he confirmed there were 30 members of Arkan's unit in Kosovo, that they'd been in Kosovo Polje and that they had allegedly killed an elderly couple there. You didn't know anything about that in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that same meeting we have evidence that General Pavkovic mentioned bodies being found in Jezerce and Rade Markovic acknowledged that was a village in an area under the JSO's responsibility and that in fact Legija had been there. You didn't know about either?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- did Trajkovic work in the same building with you in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if he could specify. There are several Trajkovics that are in the police structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is the Trajkovic connected with the SAJ, the S-A-J, who we saw listed in Exhibit P1505 earlier this morning. Do you know who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He wasn't with us. He was with his own special unit stationed in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And speaking of crimes alleged against RDB personnel, you were aware about the allegations that Milorad Nisevic from Suva Reka was charged in connection with some war crimes in that area during the war? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war we were not aware of that. And as for the alleged crimes in Suva Reka, I found out about that much, much later after the war from press reports and other media. I heard proceedings were started and certain individuals were arrested and charged with crimes in Suva Reka. During the war we didn't know that, and as I said, I only found out after retirement. I didn't even know about it for the time when I was still employed until 2001. I read about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard that I think you took a couple of trips to Belgrade in connection with Mr. Rugova, but other than that, during the war in Kosovo were you in Pristina the whole time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Pristina all the time except for when I travelled with Rugova to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were in Pristina -- we've had evidence from some Pristina Albanians who indicated that they were -- they were forced out of their home by -- by Serb forces and directed to the train station where they got on the trains and were taken to the border with Macedonia. You were in town all that time. Didn't you see hundreds or thousands of the Kosovo Albanian civilians being directed to the train station by Serb police and/or Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in Pristina, and I did see columns of Albanians that were moving towards the railway station and the bus station in order to leave from Kosovo and Metohija. I did not see anyone forcing them to go from Kosovo and Metohija. I know another thing too. Directly from Rade Markovic a few days after the departure started, Rade Markovic called me and said, "Joksic, tell the colleagues down there if I don't find them, tell the colleagues from the public security sector to prevent the departure of Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija by all means." That is the direct order that I received from Rade Markovic. I conveyed that later to General Lukic. We tried. We called these check-points at the border that they should be returned, and we even had this terrible misfortune that we were telling people to go back, and then afterwards during the course of the night they would be bombed by NATO aircraft. So they were hurt more than had they left for Albania. I think there were two or three cases like that. So in spite of all our efforts during the boarding onto trains at the railway station and there at the border where there were our check-points and where people were trying -- well, people were frightened, and for the most part, they would leave Kosovo and Metohija. I'm saying that I know this one time that General Markovic called me and said that we should try to do everything to prevent these departures. We didn't want to apply force, and we were not in a position to apply force to stop them, but we were trying to persuade people. However, we proved to be unsuccessful. So quite a few of them crossed over either into Albania or Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So when was this phone call approximately? What date?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was in the beginning of April. Maybe one of those days since I went to Belgrade with Rugova on the 1st of April and then I came back. So perhaps it was after the 5th or 6th of April. He actually insisted on the fact that they had received information that quite a few people were leaving Kosovo and Metohija and that we should do whatever we could in order to keep them there. I know that from the political organs there, I mean we were giving these refugees food. It was the provisional Executive Council. Doctors went there to treat people, to give them medication, but it was hard to keep them from leaving Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So how is it that Rade Markovic, the chief of the DB, thinks that he or you can direct the public security side about what to do? I thought the two were separate.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two separate sectors, but what he said to me was that probably the leadership of the RDB in Kosovo and Metohija would get the same instruction but he conveyed this to me and at that particular moment there was no one there from the public security and he told me to convey it to them and they would get direct instructions from their own leadership, from their chief of section or from the minister, whoever, but he told me that I should convey that everything should be done to have people stay there, not leave Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your earlier answer you said you conveyed this answer from Markovic to General Lukic. So did you do that because you understood him to have authority over the public security guys in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, not because of that. Quite simply this was conveyed to me and that I should make him aware of what the message was. It wasn't an order. Rade Markovic could not issue orders to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, your answer, and I'm reading from the English translation, page 38, starting at line 16, "Directly from Rade Markovic a few days after the departure started Rade Markovic called me and said, 'Joksic, tell the colleagues down there if I don't find them, tell the colleagues from the public security sector to prevent the departure of Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija by all means.' That is the correct order that I received from Rade Markovic. I conveyed that later to General Lukic." That's what you said before. Are you wanting to change your answer now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I stated was that I received orders for myself to take all measures, that the service should take all measures that they could. I mean and that in cooperation with colleagues from the RJB measures should be taken and that they -- well, I didn't say this here now but they would specifically receive instructions probably from their own leadership. And he conveyed to me that the service should do whatever it can, in cooperation with the RJB to stop the columns of refugees leaving Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one of the reasons he conveyed that message to you to pass on to public security was because the public security were directing the people to leave, directing the Kosovo Albanians civilians to leave Pristina; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This question has no bases in the testimony of this witness and is being presented purely argumentatively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That certainly seems to me to be a perfectly legitimate question in the context, so you may ask that question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll ask it again, Mr. Joksic. One the reasons Rade Markovic conveyed that message to you to pass on to public security was because the public security were the ones directing the people to leave, the Kosovo Albanians to leave Pristina; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. That is your opinion. No one gave them instructions to leave Pristina as far as I know. And it is not correct that that was done by the public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked about Shaun Byrnes and some of his contacts with the KLA. You mentioned in -- at page 21961 on Friday that, "We do have that information in relation to Shaun Byrnes. We have -- we also have information out there that is an integral part of a statement in the investigative proceedings where he was giving them advice," meaning the KLA. You said: "I remember this particular unit in the Lab area and he was saying they were well-equipped, well-trained and that they should keep it for the future." So from that document, as I gather, you just knew that he met with them. You didn't know specifically what was discussed between them, do you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We did know what it was that they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have tape recordings of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reading the reports, we probably had recordings, too, but I wouldn't be sure of that now. I'm telling you now about what was stated in the information that was written by our operatives. There could have been two sources of knowledge in relation to the conversations. They either had eavesdropping equipment or one of our collaborators may have been planted there and he could have been listening in on the conversation. I cannot say exactly what the source was of this information, but it's one of those two. That must be correct, because we were following the activities of the KLA and there in that brigade we had our own collaborators who reported to us about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your interpretation of that conversation was that Shaun Byrnes was encouraging them to save their good equipment and their good unit for what was going to happen in the future, the big planned offensive in the spring; right? That's your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that it might be an equally good interpretation that Shaun Byrnes was legitimately trying to reduce the violence and maintain the peace and buy time for the negotiations in Rambouillet and Paris to work? Isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, no. Knowing the overall situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. That's all I needed.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your lawyer can ask on redirect if he wants to follow that up. You were monitoring Shaun Byrnes. Were you also trying to monitor General Clark and Naumann in October 1998 when they were in Serbia trying to negotiate with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they were doing that, but I don't know about that, because at that time I was in Kosovo and Metohija, and if they are the right kind of service, they probably did that up there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean your service, the DB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But -- so you weren't aware in October 1998 or even up to the war in 1999 what Mr. Milosevic had told Clark and Naumann about how he proposed to take care of the Kosovo problem?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that. The president of the country did not inform us lower-ranking officials about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, is it a good for the break? I need to go to another document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break now. We have to break at this stage, Mr. Joksic. We will resume in half an hour. Meanwhile could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. And we will sit again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge, while the witness is coming in I just wanted to raise one procedural matter. We have a transcript of General Lukic's interview with the OTP. The original was English only, the same situation we had with the Lazarevic interview. We now have a merged version with B/C/S and English. We would like to attach it in e-court to Exhibit number P948, because we previously referred to the original version with English only and made some references to page numbers, so it will be helpful to have both and we seek leave to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to that course of action? Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, we will authorise that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, I want to ask you about another document. This is P1990. With the usher's help I will hand you a hard copy.
