This is dated the 17th of February, 1999, and it's a meeting of the Pristina MUP staff, minister of the interior, and Generals Djordjevic and Markovic as well as General Stojilkovic are in attendance and your boss Mr. Vilotic also attended. Have you seen that document before today or do you remember this meeting from February 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen this document until today. I don't remember this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to direct your attention to -- to page 3 in the B/C/S. It's page 5 in the English, Your Honours. And Mr. Joksic, I will tell you that the speaker that this is credited to is -- is the minister Stojiljkovic. Do you see a part that's highlighted in orange on your page there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm reading from the English translation. The top of page 3, the third line: "We are counting on phases of pressure. Within two or three days of an attack," and this is talking about a NATO attack, "we have to put our plans in motion and use the time to mop up the territory from terrorists." Do you recall that being discussed or do you recall see anything in writing about that, that part of the plan was if and when NATO attacked the immediate plans were to try and get rid of all the terrorists in those first few days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could go to the -- to the last page. There are a number of points raised, and the second one up from the bottom talks about raise -- we're on page 6 of the English, raise discipline, behaviour, and appearance of policemen to a high level. Do away with Rambo-style caps and bandannas. Were you aware that that was a problem with the police in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then let me turn to another topic. You were questioned by Mr. Petrovic yesterday about Mr. Rugova. At page 21987, you said there was a big media campaign and speculation about whether had he was alive or not. You told us you consulted with Vilotic as to what you should do and the two of you agreed that you should go to Rugova's house and contact him. Did you receive no instruction or direction from above, or was this your original idea between you and Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment it was only our idea because we knew about all these problems. When we found out that he was in his house and that he was alive, we thought we should go there and talk to him and ask him whether he would be prepared to state in public that he's alive, that he wasn't even wounded. So it was our decision at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before going to his house to ask him about that did you consult with Rade Markovic or any of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Only after having gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you went there who went? Was it just you or you and Vilotic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the service it was only I, and I took along with me the director of the media centre in Pristina that was in the Grand Hotel. I know his last name was Urosevic. I told you the first day that I'm not very good with names. My memory doesn't serve me well there. But Urosevic was his last name. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've heard some evidence about that and we probably know who you're talking about. You said at page 21987, line 15, that when you got there you found several members of the public security in front of the house. Did you -- did you have any conversation with them the first time you went there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just asked, is Mr. Rugova in the house? They said yes. And I went into the house and established contact with Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many public security people were there at the house when you went that first time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember exactly now, but say around five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know when and how they came to be there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you -- were you in civilian clothes or did you wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- did these guys recognise you or did you show them some kind of identification? How was it that they just let you in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had spent a lot of time in Kosovo and Metohija, I think that they recognised me. But when I passed by them I introduced myself. I said that I was Ljubivoje Joksic from the state security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you carry a weapon, a sidearm?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you mentioned you spoke to Dr. Rugova. Eventually you went back to the press centre and brought the journalist over and he gave a statement about being alive and well. You went on to tell us at page 21988 that after that press conference you agreed with your colleagues from state security that they shouldn't be inside Rugova's house. Had any of them been inside the house when you got there that first day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived on the first day they were in front of the house, and when you just walk into the house there is this entrance hall and then there's this door where there was a room where in the previous days Rugova held press conferences. I know that from TV. On one wall there were photographs of Rugova with Mother Teresa, Pope John Paul and others. So I remember seeing that room on those -- on TV from those press conferences. There were public security men there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, that question was translated as, "You agreed with your colleagues from state security that they shouldn't be inside Rugova's house"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's what his answer says in the transcript. I -- I think I should clear that up because I understood he probably meant public security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you told us that on Friday did you mean that you agreed with the guys from public security that they shouldn't be inside the house? The answer was previously transcribed as state security, but I think you meant you talked to your colleagues from public security and agreed that they shouldn't be inside the house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I established contact with Rugova, Mr. Rugova, when I went into the house, when I talked to him and when he agreed to make a statement at a press conference, when I went out there I talked to the chief of the sector in Pristina, the state security, and he gave me two operatives from the state security. So it is from that moment that they entered the entrance hall. Men in civilian clothing. They entered the entrance hall, whereas the colleagues from the public security were the external security of Rugova's house. So from that moment when I showed up and when I agreed with Rugova that he would hold a press conference, I provided for two operatives from the state security who were in the entrance hall close to where the press conference would be held and also later on when we secured the house of Rugova. However, our colleagues from the public security, we agreed with them that they had nothing more to do there any longer so they were only external security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, so when you got there that first day, there were a couple of public security guys inside the house in that entryway near where Rugova sometimes held press conferences?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you said you spoke with the chief of your sector about that and agreed that you should have state security guys inside the house, not public security; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was that? Is that -- that you spoke to, the chief --

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the centre, Milan Lakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And who did you -- who did you talk to on the public security side to tell them, "Take your guys out," or did you just tell those two guys who were there to go outside? How did that transpire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that just then I said that they should not be in the house. I said it right there, because there's a big family there, lots of children. They should go out. They did listen to me. They obeyed me, although it was not for me to give them any orders but we simply agreed as human beings. And then later on through the chief the centre I reached this agreement. I mean, he and the chief of SUP in Pristina agreed that they would provide for the external security of Ibrahim Rugova's house. So that functioned all this time for a month and even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you -- when did you report about this to -- to your superior in -- in Belgrade? Was it after the press conference was held?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the press conference was held, I called the chief of sector and I informed him about what we'd been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say chief of sector, do you mean the chief of sector in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The one in Belgrade, Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then you told us about when Mr. Sainovic came to Pristina, and I think that first time you said, at page 21989: "He arrived that evening. He contacted me, and they spoke in Rugova's house. I took him to Rugova's house and they spoke." How was it that Sainovic got in touch with you? Do you know who told him that you were the one to talk to about seeing Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all I need to clarify this. On the 1st of April, I took Mr. Rugova to Belgrade and put him in contact with the president, Slobodan Milosevic. So contact was established. You hadn't asked me about that, so I won't be explaining now. I flew back to Pristina I think on the 4th of April. I got a phone call from Rade Markovic, the chief of sector, and he said the vice-president of the federal government Sainovic would be there to talk to Rugova, please take him to Rugova because Sainovic didn't know where he was. He said to welcome him on arrival and take him there, and this is precisely what happened on the evening of the 4th he arrived in Pristina. I met up with Mr. Sainovic and I took him to Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, it's for the transcript. It's page 51, line 12. And full stop now. It's not the same sentence that I went to Pristina I think on the 4th of April. I think these are two different sentences and they confer an entirely different meaning on what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Joksic, that you went to Belgrade on the 1st of April. When did you fly back to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it was the 4th of April that Markovic telephoned you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st of April. I returned to Pristina on the 1st with Rugova and Markovic called me on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on that first trip to Belgrade did you drive or did you fly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the car it was you and Rugova and Merovci and another person from the DB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, when -- when Rade Markovic called you a few days after this return from Belgrade, why was it he contacting you about this? He didn't contact Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was the one who was involved in this context with Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who had made that decision that you would be the one? Was that because you'd been the first one to go out there that day on the 1st of April, 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because I was the first to get in touch with him. I was the first to talk to him, and we had agreed that he would call that press conference, and he had agreed to go to Belgrade with me to see President Milosevic. That was probably why I was then to continue working with Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who made the -- who made the initial decision that you should be the one to go to the house? Was that your idea or Vilotic's idea or a joint idea?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vilotic and I decided this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and do you know why the two of you decided you should be the one?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because one of our tasks was to try and find the leaders of those political parties, well-known people, to make sure they were safe and to keep them out of harm's way. The chief of sector had given us that assignment earlier on when we found out that Rugova was there, this was a good opportunity to get in touch with him straight away just to keep him out of harm's way. As I testified on Friday, Mr. Rugova was receiving threats all the time from the KLA that he would be liquidated even earlier on even prior to 1998 and in the course of 1998 and also early in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I don't think you really answered my question. It is why did the two of you decide you should be the one? Had you had any prior dealings with Mr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it because you'd been in Kosovo longer or is it because you're sort of a physically imposing guy with a deep voice?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not the reason. The reason was that I happened to be there. I had been in Kosovo for a long time. Well, that was the reason. The two of us were talking about this, but then Vilotic decides it by saying, You go and finish the job. There was no special reason for me being the one. It could have been anyone else really.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've told us then on the next page that you think that Sainovic came three or four times and you took him to see Rugova and they would talk and then he would go back to Belgrade. Did you -- did you report internally in the DB about these meetings? Did you write any reports about it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us that you did not attend all those talks between Sainovic and Rugova. I think your answer was for the most part over 70 per cent of them, and then you described the atmosphere at those meetings that you thought they both did their best to create an atmosphere of mutual trust and confidence and there were never any bad words or serious conflicts, but you can only speak about the meetings you attended. You don't know what transpired between them when you weren't there, obviously; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that's right, but neither of them ever told me after that that they had disagreed on anything. As for direct talks with Rugova, I think I had attended over 70 per cent. It's just a ballpark figure that I'm giving you. Maybe there were times when I wasn't there, but for the most part I was there for these talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you -- did you attend conversations between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But during all this time up until arrangements were made for Mr. Rugova and Mr. Merovci and their families to leave, basically their family was under house arrest, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a meeting with President Milutinovic, and you said -- yeah. You mentioned that your chief of service called you about arrangements for Mr. Rugova and Merovci to be brought to Belgrade so they can depart the country. That's Rade Markovic you're talking about in that context?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And in your answer at page 21995, this is the English translation. You said: "And we took Rugova with his family, because in the meantime when we realised that he would be released -- or, rather, that he would be taken abroad, I organised two jeeps to transfer his family from Kosovo to Belgrade." I suggest you were correct the first time when you said, "When we realised that he would be released," because in effect he was being held there, in your view, I suppose to protect him from the KLA, but he wasn't free to leave unless you all gave him permission; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Before we found him, he was too afraid to leave his home until we found out where he was. Rugova was the one who refused to leave. There was no house arrest of any kind. And another thing that proves this is the fact that Merovci who would go there came and went as he pleased. He would go to Skopje, he would walk around Pristina looking for Rugova's associates. Therefore it is not true at all that he was under any sort of house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you answered my question before and said you didn't know how or when the public security police had arrived at his house and were around the house. You don't know how long they'd been there, do you, before the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 31st when I went there to talk to Rugova, they were there. Prior to the 31st of March I don't know if they were there or not. I don't believe that they were. That's when I said that they should leave the entrance hall and that they should secure the house from outside. And I brought two state security operatives later on who then stood guard at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But the police during the external security after -- after your arrival, these are police in uniforms with weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Long-barrelled guns?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. I think automatic ones. Yes, rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and neither Mr. Rugova nor his family were allowed outside the house during all that time except before arrangements were made for them to leave the country, right, except when Mr. Rugova was taken to Belgrade for a couple of meetings. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They themselves refused to leave the house. They were too afraid to leave the house. Both Mr. Rugova and Merovci asked for the house to be guarded and their entire families to be guarded, both Rugova and Merovci. It was their personal request that we [Realtime transcript read in error "they"] should guard the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that when you first arrived and had a couple of your security men set up outside that there was a German journalist, a female German journalist in Rugova's house?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry for the interruption, but 57, 1, it was their personal request that we should guard the house, not they should guard the house. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Through, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Joksic. Were you not aware that there was a German journalist, a woman named Renate Flottau F-l-o-t-t-a-u, I believe, in Mr. Rugova's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't know that at the time. At the time we didn't know that this lady was there nor did they tell us that she was there. There were quite a number of his family members and relatives that I wasn't inclined to go to each and every room just to check who was there. He said there are 17 of us here. I took that for granted and I didn't go to any of the rooms. The Albanians can be a bit peculiar in this respect, the women, you know, that sort of thing, so men don't go to those rooms upstairs. I know about this particular custom that they had, and that's why I was not inclined to go to any of the rooms to check. They told me that there were 17 of them there. I took that at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you really didn't need to worry about that because they were all going to be kept there and only allowed outside if and when you, and I mean you collectively, the police, the DB and the JB, permitted it. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that during the war communications were bad for your service, but you told us that in connection with Mr. Rugova you did manage to connect another phone so he could stay in contact with the rest of the world, for example, with Hill in Skopje and other officials; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it those conversations were probably closely monitored? That would be standard practice with your service, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was standard practice. It's just it was very difficult to organise at the time. The reason being the telecommunication installations had been destroyed from which this could have been done. Therefore, I'm not sure that those conversations were eavesdropped on, the conversations that Rugova had from his home. The post office in Pristina had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a question. This is from the Bench. I have a question. What were your own views about Dr. Rugova, because you travelled with him to Belgrade. You establish a contact. What did you think of him as a -- as a person and as a politician or whatever? Can you give us some views, your personal views? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got an impression during my years of life and work down there. He struck me as a person who wasn't difficult to talk to and someone that politicians could negotiate with. But throughout those eight years, every Friday he would give a press conference. At the end of each and every one of these he would say that DSK, his political party was in favour of a neutral and independent Kosovo. I was aware of his attitude throughout those eight years. Every Friday whenever he was in Pristina he would give a press conference and say the same thing, he was in favour of a neutral and independent Kosovo. Now that the war had begun and victims were falling on either side of the conflict, he softened up a bit and my impression now was that he believed there should be negotiations, that the war should stop, and that there should be a chance to talk about these relationships in Kosovo and Metohija. My impression during those days when I was taking him to Belgrade a number of times was that he was prepared to negotiate, unlike some other leaders of Kosovo Albanians who advocated the use of force as the only means to resolving the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I have a single question that stems from Mr. Hannis's cross-examination. This was never brought up on examination-in-chief. Therefore, there was no need for me to ask the question in my cross-examination. It's about this witness's evidence last Friday. Mr. Hannis asked him about meetings in 1998. It was exchange of information between the MUP and the army and the witness claims to have attended a couple of those and then the question came who did you see there and then the witness said General Lazarevic and Pavkovic from the MUP. The meetings were held at the corps command or at the MUP building and the only thing I wish to ask the witness is whether perhaps he can pinpoint the time period in 1998 when he saw General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just one moment before we -- are you referring to the evidence we heard today on this? You say Friday. We certainly had some evidence today about meetings with Lazarevic and Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was today about 1998 and last Friday Mr. Hannis when he first began --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one today was about 1999, but are you asking about 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, because last Friday, I am sure my friend Mr. Hannis remembers, this was brought up at the start of his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I remember him answering today about meeting Pavkovic and Lazarevic in 1999, but in 1998 I thought it was just a general VJ-MUP get together, and I don't think I asked about names or heard those names, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a page reference for this, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can hunt and raise the matter at the end of re-examination, and if it causes any difficulty for Mr. Ivetic, he will have a chance to come back on it, but if you find the page reference, we can consider that at the end of his re-examination. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think I've found it at page 22010, line 3. And the answer was, "Well, as for those that I attended, General Lazarevic and Pavkovic and then from June or July 1998 onwards General Sreten Lukic and one of his staff." So that may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. You can ask your question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, just a single question from me about 1998. You heard, didn't you. At what point in time did you see General Lazarevic at these meetings with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I don't think I'm wrong, in the first three or four months I did not see General Lazarevic. Perhaps he was away somewhere. Between January and April I didn't see him. It wasn't until May or June that I started seeing General Lazarevic. In Pristina. At meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day again, Mr. Joksic, I'll try and be brief. Today Mr. Hannis asked you about other possible interpretations of Mr. Shaun Byrnes' actions and words and you started to answer him and Mr. Hannis did not care for your answer. Could you please continue with what you were going to say about the reasons why for you there was no possibility of interpreting Shaun Byrnes' actions and deeds in any other way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, well, we were monitoring Mr. Shaun Byrnes' activities. We had a lot of information, a lot of other reports indicating that he was lending his support to members of the KLA and advising them on what to do, when to attack, when not to attack, and so on and so forth. I can't recall any details. There was a flood of incoming reports and our operatives were writing these reports every day and submitting them. I read a lot about that, and I do know that there was quite some information pointing out the links between Shaun Byrnes on the one hand and members of the KLA on the other. When I analysed those reports my impression was that he was some sort of an advisor to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could have Exhibit P1811 on the screen. This is a document that Mr. Hannis showed you today. And, sir, you testified that you did recognise most of the people listed in this decision. The question I have for you, sir, is are any of the persons listed herein as members of the MUP staff employees of the State Security Service, the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And then the other day you testified during cross-examination that during the bombing you spent a lot of time with General Lukic as the MUP moved around to avoid being killed by NATO. Did you have occasion to see any generals of the RJB who were always with Lukic during this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. For the most part it was General Obrad Stevanovic, the assistant minister, and sometimes General Djordjevic would come to Pristina, too, from the RJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joksic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for your time and your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the document on the screen at the moment, that is P1811, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It says at the bottom of that page in English "Chiefs of secretariats of the interior and of the RDB centres and departments in Kosovo ... are hereby designated members of the staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the same general language from the prior decision but he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- talking, I believe about the named individuals who Mr. Hannis asked him about and who I asked if any of those were members of the RDB. On the Serbian those would be the first full page and the first four lines on the second page. I don't have the English in front of me to see. I suspect you're talking about the next set of paragraphs that come after that before the end of the second page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. You just need to look at the paragraph immediately after the one you've drawn his --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- attention to. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It would be Cedo Sakic. JUDGE: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please give us your full name for the record and tell us briefly about your career.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: My name is Cedo Sakic, born on the 20th of January, 1956, in a place called Lipovo Polje, Gospic municipality, the Republic of Croatia. I was admitted in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia on the 15th of December 1977. I worked there until the 1st of July 2000 when I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What jobs did you do in 1999?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: In 1999 I was chief of the escort service in the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to start from the beginning. I said -- we'll move right away to the topic of our interest. Let me ask you, did you go to Kosovo and Metohija accompanied by Bozidar Protic, and if you did, how many times?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I say how many times, I meant how many times with him when he drove trucks from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: In 1999, I went four times accompanied by Bozidar Protic. He was my -- I was his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On whose orders did you go the first time as Protic's escort?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The first time I provided security for Mr. Bozidar Protic I received the order from my superior officer, the command of the unit for security of republican organs Colonel Mladen Sipovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It came into the record as I asked you the first time. Did you say the first time or every time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go the first time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Late in April was the first time when I received the order from my commander to provide security to Mr. Protic, and we went to Pristina. In fact, I believe it was some sort of utility enterprise or maybe a marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you go, with which vehicle, from Belgrade to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: We used two vehicles, Puh, a Mercedes, M601565 and M601564 were the licence plates. Those were issued personally to me. They were the vehicles of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you use any other vehicles apart from these?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: On the way there we didn't use any other vehicles, just the ones issued personally to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who sat in the same car as you when you went to Pristina for the first time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The driver Jovan Pecenica. I was the passenger next to the driver. Mr. Bozidar Protic sat behind me, and next to him was a policeman nicknamed Boske. I don't remember his full name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is Puh some reference to a type of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what were the two vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain what a Puh is?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: It's an all-terrain, vehicle, a jeep. On our local market it was called Puh. In the Western markets it was called Mercedes 230 diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned someone named Boske. Was he regularly a part of your group or was he seconded to you occasionally?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: This policeman Boske, he worked in a different section, but he was seconded to me for a long time as assistance, and I can't really remember for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was in the other vehicle?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The driver was Ljubinko Banjac. Next to him sat Dragan Stosic, who was also one of the officers. Then Dragan Jankovic sat behind him. He wasn't from my unit. I know he was from Paracin, and I can't remember his exact name. And the fourth was Vlastimir Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said Dragan Jankovic and I can't remember his name. Do you mean to say you were not sure?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I believe it was Dragan, but I'm not sure. And Dragan Stosic was certainly an officer in the second vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did Protic talk to anyone in the car on the way?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Two, three times as we were travelling Mr. Protic talked to someone on his cell phone. He was just -- he just said the exact location where we were at the time and said nothing further. I didn't know who he was talking to. I asked him why he was discovering our position. I reminded him we were in a state of war, that we were being listened to, but he simply avoided an answer. He didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you arrived in Pristina, and what happens then?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: We took a roundabout way from Devet Jugovica towards Obilic from the juncture, and we entered Pristina near Caglavica, near the petrol station. Since we didn't know the town well, he told us exactly where to go because he knew the exact location. He took us there. We stopped. Mr. Protic and I got out of the car -- can I go on? The security detail there consisted of people in civilian clothes and some in uniform. Mr. Protic greeted those who were in uniform -- or, rather, one of them. However, at that parking lot there were two refrigerator lorries. One of those had the refrigerator working and the other not. The other one was open and empty. Mr. Protic got into the truck because the key was in the ignition, in the refrigerator truck. He explained to me that he needed to create pressure to pump air, so to speak, as he explained to me. He got into the second refrigerator lorry, took the tool box, and put it in the refrigerator lorry he was going to drive. There were some other vehicles on that parking lot, probably impounded in various incidents. From one of the jeeps he took a white spade and put it in his lorry. I noted all that in my notepad and later put it in my report submitted to my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion while you were in Pristina, did Protic from any location whatsoever telephone anyone from a land-line?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic had had no opportunity and did not speak to anyone from a land-line, and he didn't need to because he had a cell phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion while you were in Pristina did he tell you to whom he had spoken while you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: As we were going around that truck, he wanted to speak to me one-on-one. When we were behind that refrigerator lorry which had the refrigerator on, he told me he had spoken to General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was Protic's superior at the time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: His superior was General Zekovic, Gojko, whose last name I don't remember, and Mr. Nenadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time was it usual for drivers under Nenadic to have cell phones?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I know that drivers under Nenadic had been issued with cell phones back in December 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean to say 1998?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the call-sign or code number of these cell phones given to this category of drivers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Their first numbers, first digits, were 063, because that provider covered all of Serbia, whereas the one beginning with 064 had coverage only next to the motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far did you accompany Protic on your way back from Pristina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: We accompanied him up to the petrol station near the building of MUP of Serbia -- or, rather, the building of emergency medical service. We left him there and said good-bye, and he hung back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say up to the emergency medical service building or the MUP building, you mean in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade, and prior to that we had stopped in Velika Plana where he told us not to accompany him further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the first time. How long was it before you travelled with Protic again? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the same week, maybe five, six, or seven days later. We also went to Pristina, again on the orders of my superior commander, Mr. Sipovac Mladen, again to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you use the same vehicles?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The very same vehicles. And it was the same security team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you pick up Protic and how did you arrange where to pick him up?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The first time we started around 1400 hours. The second time we departed around 1800 hours. On that occasion my commander announced to me that I was again to be the security man for Protic. However, at that time Protic called me from his cell phone to meet up next to the emergency medical service building next to a business called Stek, between the petrol station and the Stek business, that we would meet there, that we should drive up to there and pick him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he again with you in the same car or in the other car?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: He was in my car, sitting behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many other policemen were there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: In the first vehicle there was Jovan Pecenica, the driver, and Boske sitting behind the driver as the fourth man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of assignment did Protic get this time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I asked him where we were going and he said directly to Pristina. But again, on the way he gave someone the location where we were but only from Celija Lake to Pristina. And he guided us again in a roundabout way from the other side of town so that we entered Pristina from Caglavica. He took us to the back of the building of Rilindija newspaper where there was a wire-fenced parking lot. At the very entrance to the parking lot there was a booth with a policeman inside who was guarding the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said he communicated your location to someone. Using what equipment?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: His cell phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You arrived in Pristina to that parking lot near Rilindija that was guarded. On that occasion did Protic, while you were in Pristina, that is, have the possibility of calling someone from a land-line, and did he phone anyone using a land-line in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic had no possibility to call anyone using a land-line, and he did not call anyone. He didn't use a land-line telephone at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first time and the second time when you were in Pristina, did he enter any buildings in Pristina and, if so, what buildings?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic did not enter a single building in Pristina, and he could not go anywhere from us because I was his escort. He couldn't go away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did he take over the truck then?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in that parking lot, the policeman who was there in the hut got up and lifted the barrier. We drove in. Mr. Protic got out of the vehicle and came to this duty policeman. I don't know what it was he talked about with him, and then he returned into the car that was air-conditioned. He sat in the truck, turned it on. The engine was working for about five minutes. He went around the vehicle and went back. He talked to someone then on the telephone, but I don't know who, and he turned on his lights in this way showing us that we could leave, and that is exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not air-conditioning but refrigeration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it the reference now to the refrigerated vehicle is to a lorry and not a car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, you said that he was talking on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of telephone was it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic used his own cell phone in the truck of -- in this refrigeration truck. Refrigerator truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who it was that he talked to then?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't hear because I was outside, and I don't know what it was that he was talking about or who it was that he was talking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went back to Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Belgrade. So where did you leave Protic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: When returning to Belgrade, 100 kilometres away from Belgrade there is a gasoline station in Velika Plana. We stopped there to refresh ourselves a bit and that's where we stopped and then we continued to Belgrade and Protic told us to accompany him only to the emergency hospital -- rather, the MUP, and then that's what we did, and he went further on to Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the second time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify a couple of matters from this? On this second occasion, did you go to Pristina in two motor vehicles again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the same eight people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how many refrigerated trucks were there in the car park on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this occasion I pointed out that it was only one refrigerator truck in that parking lot. In the first one there were two. One was open, the back door was open, whereas this one was closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the first occasion what happened to the other refrigerated truck, the one that Protic did not drive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just try to move on a bit further to clarify the points that Judge Bonomy was interested in. Did this truck stay behind in the parking lot when you left Pristina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The second refrigerator truck remained in the parking lot. It was empty. I don't know what happened to it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the third time that you accompanied Protic, and where was it that you went? And I'd like to call up on e-court 6D1494. While we're waiting for the map, can you tell us where it was that you went the third time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The third time we went to Kosovska Mitrovica via Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After how many days?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, this was about 20 days perhaps. Say 21 or 19. I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After what?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: After the second time I accompanied him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What vehicle were you in?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I was in the vehicles that I'd been issued in the unit. These were Puh jeeps, the ones that I explained about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Protic? What vehicle did he take?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Protic drove some kind of a truck. Sort of like a refrigerator truck. I don't know now. It didn't have the thing up there for refrigeration. It didn't have a device for refrigeration. It was just sort of like a big box.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the truck where Protic was?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, when I went to Kosovo I would go in to see him, and I'd ride with him for about a hundred kilometres roughly. When we got off the highway near Krusevac until we passed the lake of Celija. I was keeping him company because he was bored.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I need a map, it probably takes more time for it to be uploaded, and I need to ask you questions about that map, but then perhaps I can ask you other questions until the map is there. When you reached Pristina, where did you go and how?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Five kilometres before Pristina, around five kilometres before Pristina at Devet Jugovica we turned right, and then we went to Milosevo. In Milosevo there is this crossroads leading to Obilic and then going left to Kosovo Polje or the other side of Pristina, that is, and to the right you go to Kosovska Mitrovica. When we got there I didn't know where it was that we would be going after that. Protic was signalling us where to go, to turn right. As we went on, he was just giving us indications that we should move faster, faster, flashing his lights. And we got to Kosovska Mitrovica and then he took us to this railway station, and then there is a timber processing plant close to it. The door was open, so we could see. I mean, we could see these machines, the machines that carpenters use. So that is how I came to the conclusion that that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now we have the map on our screens, so I would kindly ask the usher to help you with the pen, and could you please mark your route on this map, where it was that you were driving as you went from Belgrade to Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The number of this exhibit? 6D1494. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the map is in Cyrillic, to the right of various localities could you please use numbers. Number 1, Pristina, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Does this apply to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now Obilic, number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 3, Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: May I explain a bit more?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: There is this one village here and this other village there. This is Donja Brnjica and then Gornja Brnjica up to Pristina, near Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Use number 3 to mark Kosovska Mitrovica. 4 and 5 the villages, and give us the names again as you put the numbers there.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the village number for?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Donja Brnjica. And number 5 is Gornja Brnjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have the IC number for this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is number 5, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on the left-hand side from number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's just the big red blob. Okay. You can have a number then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a big village.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC 185, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we've already marked this exhibit, we can no longer draw things on it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can call it up and you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: IC185, and then you can draw on it once it's there on the screen in its photographed form.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call IC185. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sakic, could you please mark for us here the direction from which you came. Did you come from the direction of Podujevo? Can you just link this up to the blue line? [In English] Too late now. Okay. That's fine. And can I have --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could I have the IC number for this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, we lawyers sometimes have to put questions that may sound illogical, but I have to ask you this: On the occasion when you went to Kosovska Mitrovica, during your third trip, that is, accompanying Protic in relation to the escort of the truck, did you turn off and go to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: No. We never went to Pristina because it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already explained to us that you came to Kosovska Mitrovica, this timber processing plant. And what did Protic do with the truck that he drove?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic drove his truck to that entranceway. He backed off and parked it in a way that the front of the truck was parallel to the door of this timber processing plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did you see what it was that Protic was loading onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see because I was on the other side, and on the other side to where I was, there was the railway station and the ramp for loading train cars. Since we were looking from up there, we had no chance to see any of this. And Protic was with us up there later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Protic making a telephone call from there from a land-line?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Protic had no chance to make a telephone call from there and talk to anyone because there wasn't a land-line telephone there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? Was Protic there with you within that area? Where did he go to?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: He came to us. Mr. Protic came to us, and I think there could have been up to ten people there including those who were loading whatever they were loading. The rest were policemen. And we talked about all sorts of things there. Mr. Protic came to us and he was with us, and it was the -- probably of the commander, leader of these men who were there. I don't know. He had the rank of captain, and he happened to be there and he talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did you ask this captain?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I asked him, "What is being loaded there."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what did the captain answer to you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The captain said, "We are loading Siptars." And in response to my question "What do you mean Siptars, who killed them," because that was quite foreign to me. And he said, "Their guys did it." I said, "What do you mean their guys," and he said to me "NATO aircraft." That was his answer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go with that truck?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: When the loading was over these people in civilian clothes called and said that it was all over. Protic went down and turned on his truck and flashed a light at us, and then we went towards Pristina and then from that crossroads to Podujevo and then further on to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did you enter Pristina on your way back?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need for us to enter Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, did you go to Kosovo and Metohija yet again escorting Protic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, towards the end of the NATO bombing. I can't remember the exact date. I was again called up by my superior to escort Protic, and then we went to Janjevo. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think we could deal with that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sakic, we have to break now for lunch. That will be for an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last thing we discussed was your trip to Janjevo. How did you get there and how did Protic get there? To Kosovo and Metohija, I mean. What sort of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: This time around we drove in our own vehicles, and Mr. Protic drove in a Tatra owned by the Gemaks company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you actually go into Protic's Tatra vehicle on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, both on the way there and on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the same people escorting him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Same vehicles, same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen on your way to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: On our way to Kosovo and Metohija, we stopped in a place called Blace, which is where the house is where Mr. Protic was born. We had coffee there. He pulled a jerrycan with oil, fuel out of the vehicle and left it in his own garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As he pressed on was there any firing along the way?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Near a place called Janjevo we came under fire from everywhere. We passed and took a right turn towards the turn-off for Obilic and Mitrovica. There is a storage facility, a warehouse where commodity reserves of the Republic of Serbia are. We stopped there to see if anyone had been injured. And we were joined here by a politician named Momo Trajkovic who also came under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that the firing took place in the village of Janjevo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Outside the village of Janjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened at Devet Jugovica?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In Devet Jugovica. I’m sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was the road to Janjevo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The road to Janjevo. Perhaps I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have 6D1494 brought back up in e-court. Not everything was recorded that we were saying a minute ago. Did the fire occur in the village of Janjevo or the village of Devet Jugovica?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Outside the village of Devet Jugovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the road to Janjevo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: On the road to Janjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll probably be spending some time waiting for the map to show up on our screens. In the meantime let me ask you this -- the map's there. Can you please show us where exactly you were moving. Can you please mark your movements on this map.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: It was like this. We went from Podujevo as far as Devet Jugovica, then as far as the crossroads, and then towards Kosovo Polje. That's the route that we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 16 JUDGE BONOMY: At the end of that -- at the end of that route is that Janjevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you put a number 1 next to Janjevo, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems a long way from Devet Jugovica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I could do anything to move it closer, I would. It's about 20 kilometres from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I ask is you said that you came under fire near place called Janjevo, but it would appear it was more than 20 kilometres from Janjevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Not in Janjevo. That's not where the firing occurred. It was in Devet Jugovica, which is round about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Put a number 2 there please at Devet Jugovica.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please explain whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: We had a shortcut to take here through Pristina, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Don't draw anything, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: However, there is a village here called Vranjevac and every time we went there we would drive around it because sometimes the Siptars brought children to the road there in order to stop us moving and then they would start sniping at us. So this was something that we had to avoid every time we drove there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll ask CLSS to translate the passage from 81, 2 to line 16. Now, what's the significance of Vranjevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vranjevac was significant because this was a densely populated area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's it got to do with this particular journey? We're looking at one event at the moment which is your fourth trip. Now, where did -- what happened at Vranjevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing happened. I'm mentioning this as a place we had to avoid and drive around it as opposed to right through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Protic -- Sakic. I'm sorry. Do you know about this period, I mean throughout 1999, was there a very important stronghold of the KLA in Vranjevo [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that precisely being the reason why we took the long way around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we see you arriving in Janjevo? What do you find when you get there? What's going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop for a moment. If you look at the question, Mr. Lukic, it says was there a very important stronghold of the KLA in -- oh, no it's now changed. It was Janjevo. But -- you gave a name that I think even I could hear ended in "jevo." Now, which place were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vranjevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Protic --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sakic, my apologies, really. We see you arriving in Janjevo?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's going on there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Right in the middle of Janjevo there was a police patrol waiting for us. They took charge of Mr. Protic and then he was gone for half an hour. There is a forest nearby, and I had no idea where he was off to from there, but during this trip he -- this was the only time he was away from me and not under my control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. When Protic returned, was he also under the escort of that patrol that took charge of him?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because he was coming from down the slope upwards, and there's a bit of a slope there and we were at the top of that slope. That's where we were standing. So first we saw a police vehicle arrive followed by the Tatra lorry which beamed its lights on us to give us a signal. So we got into our vehicle and drove on to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were driving back the same way now.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Protic? Did he stop anywhere this time around?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Protic tell you where you were going to, and where did he tell you that if he did?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: We didn't know this road that we were taking at all. Protic told me near Aleksinac when we got into his vehicle that we were on our way to Petrovo Selo because we were taking a different road, Prokuplje, Nis, and then the toll booth where he started complaining that he was to tired to keep on driving. It was 10.00 p.m. already, and so on and so forth. After about 20 kilometres I switched to his truck. I had a lunch box with me. I gave him something to eat and then we continued on to Paracin where we took a right turn and about 20 or 30 kilometres from there we stopped at a petrol station. We refreshed ourselves and pressed on for Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you write any reports in relation to these trips?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Whatever I did that I did outside Belgrade, I was under an obligation to write a report which I would then submit to my unit commander in Sipovac. Had I had failed to do that, I would have been punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention regarding the transcript, everything is recorded as a question, but from "whatever I did" is actually the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether Protic knew where he was going already while he was in Belgrade; if so, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every time you went with him, every time you escorted him these four times that you went, did you have the impression that even back in Belgrade, Protic knew where he was going?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every time I took this trip with him he had received instructions in Belgrade as to where we would be going and what we would have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I know that because he would tell us, We're off to Pristina and then as soon as we reached Devet Jugovica he would warn us by beaming his headlights at us, using long beams that something was going on and then he would point us in our next direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During these trips did Protic ever drop the name of Sreten Lukic in any way?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I am absolutely positive that he never ever mentioned General Sreten Lukic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During these trips could Protic go anywhere without being escorted by the police?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't. Mr. Protic never strayed from me at all except for the fourth trip in Janjevo where another police force, a local police force took charge of him and went with him to those hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you travelled together did you go to Protic to the Pristina SUP or the Pristina MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: The Pristina staff, the staff that was in Pristina, kept changing its location. We didn't even know where it was at the time. So we never went there simply because we didn't need to. Mr. Protic would receive all of his assignments in Belgrade and he knew exactly where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Protic phone you in 2006?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Protic in 2005. We spoke on the phone in 2006 and twice in 2007 I was with him. In 2005, on the way out of my flat at Nikolaj Gogolj 38A, I found him standing next to a removal van that he owned with another two men. I approached him and said, "Proto, is that you," and he didn't say anything but he started saying things immediately against General Lukic and he started attacking General Lukic verbally. He said the following words: "I will testify against Lukic because he did not award me a flat whereas he had awarded one to the driver Basanovic." He said, "I will testify in favour of Haradinaj, I will testify in favour of Thaci," and then I asked him, "Okay, so how come nobody's asking me anything, they're just talking to you." And then he told me. I was summoned by The Hague Tribunal, and they told me just show up and we'll give you a thousand dollars for that. I said in relation to you that the whole thing stank to high heavens and that you had run off with your team. I'm under oath. I have to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now tell us about yourself. After talking to him, were you summoned by the MUP to testify?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of April at 9.00 a.m., I was in Vladimirovac, I own a house there, just past Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the year, please, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: 2006. My phone at home rang. I returned, picked up the receiver. I heard a voice saying, "It's Proto speaking." And I said, "Say it." Proto. I thought -- since I had another friend with the surname of Protic, I thought it was the other one. And then hearing what he asked, it was -- I knew it was Bozidar Protic. He asked me, "Cedo, did you get a summons to the court? All the drivers received summons to the court regarding the refrigerator trucks. They know everything. There's no reason to hide anything." I answered, "I didn't get anything and nobody told me anything about anything, but I know one thing, an honest man need not worry. Just tell the truth." And that's what I said to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you warn him there was a written report?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I added in addition regarding every of my trips there is a detailed written report at the MUP of Serbia that I submitted after each trip on which I served as escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you invited to testify?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date, but I believe it was the 28th of September around 8.00 a.m. My cell phone rang and somebody from the administration for war crimes called me. I don't remember the name, although he told me his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the year?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SAKIC
